builder_plan.scenario: Start with one repeated product task that has a measurable failure or cost.
builder_plan.change: Read the methods and identify one change you can isolate in that workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current implementation on the same held-out tasks.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful outcomes, response time, human rework, and total cost per successful task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Steering intonational tunes in text-to-speech synthesis
summary: The method replaces prompt-based intonation control (which the paper shows mostly fails except for final punctuation) with difference-of-means steering vectors applied to the transformer backbone's hidden state during generation in RVQ-based TTS systems such as CSM and S2. It costs a small drop in predicted naturalness, requires collecting human imitations of the target tunes to compute vectors, and adds per-step intervention logic inside the generation loop; punctuation-derived vectors are simpler but degrade the voice when pushing toward assertions. It can fail to select a precise target tune beyond a broad falling or rising tendency, and the pitch accent may not follow the edge tone, so utterance-level intonation may remain internally inconsistent.
rationale: The reader can apply this at small scale on open RVQ-TTS checkpoints with a single GPU, but the benefit is workload-dependent and the residual naturalness cost and incomplete tune control require validation on their own voices and use cases before production adoption.
technique: Activation steering of prosodic intonation in RVQ text-to-speech

claims.statement: The method replaces prompt-based intonation control (which the paper shows mostly fails except for final punctuation) with difference-of-means steering vectors applied to the transformer backbone's hidden state during generation in RVQ-based TTS systems such as CSM and S2. It costs a small drop in predicted naturalness, requires collecting human imitations of the target tunes to compute vectors, and adds per-step intervention logic inside the generation loop; punctuation-derived vectors are simpler but degrade the voice when pushing toward assertions. It can fail to select a precise target tune beyond a broad falling or rising tendency, and the pitch accent may not follow the edge tone, so utterance-level intonation may remain internally inconsistent.

Steering vectors derived from human tune imitations move most generated recordings to the intended rising or falling condition in both CSM and S2, generalize across speakers, and incur a small cost in predicted naturalness; only the broad tune direction is controllable, with the edge tone responding more coherently than the pitch accent.
